Alternatives to building a new pipeline include blending hydrogen into existing natural gas pipelines, and as demand grows, retrofitting existing natural gas pipelines to operate on pure gaseous hydrogen. In the case of hydrogen blending, no capital costs would be required for hydrogen transport, but hydrogen blending limits due to factors such as natural gas pipeline material, operating pressure, and end- use application would apply. Generally, lower-grade steel pipelines are more tolerant to hydrogen exposure than high-grade steel and thus have lower risk of hydrogen embrittlement and hydrogen leakage (Topolski et al. 2022). In 2022, NLR published a report on hydrogen blending into natural gas pipeline titled Hydrogen Blending into Natural Gas Pipeline Infrastructure: Review of the State of Technology (Topolski et al. 2022). The report mentions several demonstration projects of hydrogen blending into natural gas pipelines with blends ranging from a few percent up to 100%. In the event that no natural gas pipelines to an airport are directly compatible with pure hydrogen, natural gas pipelines could be retrofitted, albeit with an associated upfront capital cost. A pipe-in-pipe approach, where a hydrogen-compatible pipeline is inserted inside of the original natural gas pipeline, is one retrofit approach. Other retrofitting techniques include admixing degradation inhibitors, or applying an inner coating to the original pipeline, but these two pathways require further investigation before commercialization (Télessy et al. 2024). For transporting hydrogen long distances and at high throughput, railways and ocean carriers are viable. These delivery pathways would make sense in the case hydrogen is sourced from international suppliers, or from a nonadjacent region of the United States, where lower-cost hydrogen production can be achieved. LH transported via rail or ocean carrier is unlikely to be 2 delivered directly to an airport and would instead be delivered to an unloading terminal or port before being piped or trucked to the airport. Liquid-hydrogen-carrying railcars and ocean tankers are still under development. Linde is designing a liquid hydrogen tank suitable for rail transport expected to be available in 2026. The tank will have a capacity of 8.7 metric tons of LH with a holding time up to 30 days (Linde 2 n.d.). Notably, a single long-haul train could have multiple of these tanks, making a single train delivery with a magnitude of 102–103 metric tons plausible.
